pr.title: Use a reduced recursion limit in the MIR inliner's cycle breaker
pr.description:
This probably papers over https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/128887, but primarily I'm opening this PR because multiple compiler people have thought about making this change which probably means it's a good idea.

r? compiler-errors
pr.author: saethlin

processing.reason: The PR (rust-lang/rust#129714) does not contain a value-level semantic transformation. It changes only the recursion budget passed by `mir_callgraph_reachable` to the inliner's internal `process` call-graph search: the historical/pre-PR code passes `tcx.recursion_limit()`, while the fix passes `tcx.recursion_limit() / 2`. Both versions are compiler-internal traversal-budget arguments, not program-visible computations. The original and transformed program semantics are identical; the only observable difference is that the unreduced budget can let the trait solver reach a fatal recursion-limit overflow before the inliner gives up, i.e. a compile-time crash-avoidance/workaround. Encoding this as two ordinary Rust functions that return different values (e.g. returning `limit` vs `limit / 2`) would not be the historical wrong transformation—it would be an unrelated arithmetic change—and no concrete input can make the actual original vs. fixed inliner produce distinct defined runtime values under Miri. Hence no source-grounded counterexample pair exists that satisfies the required harness (both passing, same inputs, different defined outputs).

analysis.originalLogic: In `mir_callgraph_reachable`, the MIR inliner's cycle breaker passed `tcx.recursion_limit()` directly as the depth/recursion budget to the `process` call-graph search. This made the inliner's traversal budget identical to the trait solver's recursion budget while the solver's type complexity grows with each call-graph recursion step.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historically incorrect behavior is retaining the full `tcx.recursion_limit()` for the inliner's call-graph reachability search (the pre-PR `-        tcx.recursion_limit(),` behavior) instead of reducing it to `tcx.recursion_limit() / 2`. With the same limit on both sides, the trait solver reaches its limit before the inliner gives up, producing a fatal overflow error rather than the inliner abandoning the inlining search.
analysis.inputDomain: Rust programs whose MIR call graph contains deeply recursive/generic calls such that the type complexity queried from the trait solver grows as the inliner recurses into the call graph. The relevant domain is MIR inlining reachability analysis, especially under the next trait solver, where solver overflow cannot yet be returned as an ordinary error.
analysis.summary: The MIR inliner's cycle breaker must use a recursion limit smaller than the trait solver's limit (`tcx.recursion_limit() / 2`) when searching the call graph. Otherwise solver type complexity can hit the shared limit first and emit a fatal overflow error instead of letting the inliner give up on inlining. This is a crash-avoidance/workaround fix, not a semantic transformation of MIR.
analysis.trigger: A deeply recursive or mutually recursive generic call graph is explored by `mir_callgraph_reachable`; as inlining recursion deepens, the trait solver's type complexity grows. If the cycle breaker uses the full compiler recursion limit, the solver reaches the limit first and fatally overflows.
preconditions: The MIR inliner runs its call-graph reachability/cycle-breaking search via `mir_callgraph_reachable`.
The program has a sufficiently deep generic/recursive call structure that the inliner's traversal approaches the recursion limit.
Trait-solver queries made during that traversal accumulate type complexity; the source notes this applies especially to `-Znext-solver`, where trait solver overflow cannot yet return an error.
pitfalls: Do not treat the reduced limit as a semantic change: it only makes the inliner stop searching earlier, so the program's behavior must remain unchanged.
Do not require that inlining still occurs at depths beyond the reduced limit; the intended behavior is to give up on finding useful MIR inlining.
Do not conflate the inliner's traversal budget with the trait solver's budget: the fix deliberately makes the inliner hit its limit first so the solver does not emit a fatal error.
Avoid asserting a specific inlining outcome in a regression test; the observable contract is successful compilation without a fatal recursion-limit error.
The division is integer division, so the effective budget is half the configured limit (for example, the source describes recursing 64 times as already unlikely to yield useful inlining).
analysis.testStrategy: Build a focused UI/compile-pass test around deeply recursive generic calls that exercise MIR inliner cycle breaking, preferably with a small explicit recursion limit to keep the test fast. Compare two compiler configurations that differ only in the cycle-breaker budget: the historical full `tcx.recursion_limit()` versus `tcx.recursion_limit() / 2`. The correct configuration should complete compilation without a fatal trait-solver recursion-limit error; the historical configuration is the failing side. Also keep a normal recursive-call case to ensure cycle handling still terminates. Do not assert that deep calls are inlined, and do not claim execution/reproduction unless the compiler was actually built and run.
